title: Secular sabbath
hookLine: some people who keep no religion keep a weekly rest

cards: Saturday morning. The laptop is in a drawer. The phone charges in another room, face down.
There's no service to attend and no candle to light, because the person in this kitchen keeps no religion at all. And still, once a week, they stop. No email, no errands, no catching up.
A long breakfast. A walk with no destination. A nap nobody earned.
Ask what they're doing and they might shrug: I'm keeping a sabbath, sort of. Some people who belong to no faith keep a weekly rest like this. The shape is borrowed.

teach.b: Back in year one, this path met Shabbat itself. The sabbath is Jewish first, and it still belongs to the Jewish people, with its own laws, prayers and meaning.
A secular sabbath borrows only its outline, and it should say so. Look at that outline in the Torah. In Deuteronomy, the command isn't only for you.
Your children rest, your animals rest, the stranger in your town rests, and the text gives the reason plainly: "that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou."
A day off only the powerful get isn't what the text describes. The rest is shared, or it isn't the thing. Then the Gospel of Mark.
Jesus is challenged about what may be done on the sabbath, and he answers, "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Christians and Jews read that line in their own ways.

teach.h: MADE FOR THE PERSON, NOT THE TASK.
teach.b: What a secular keeper takes from it is simpler: the day exists to serve a person, not to become one more task to perform well.

Third, Thoreau, at Walden: "I love a broad margin to my life." A margin is the blank space around the writing on a page. Nothing is printed there, and without it the page is a wall of text you can't read.
So a secular sabbath has three borrowed parts: a regular time that comes back each week, a rest that includes the people around you, and a margin where nothing has to be produced or proven.

how: People who keep a secular sabbath usually choose a regular weekly stretch, often a day or an evening, to set aside work, errands and screens, and spend it on meals, walks, rest and company; observant Jews keep Shabbat itself, with its own laws and prayers, from Friday sunset to Saturday night.

games.q: your rest day arrives, and you spend it tidying the house, clearing your inbox and running every errand you put off. you feel productive. is that the sabbath?
o: yes, getting things done is restful.
no, the day is a margin where nothing has to be produced.
games.why: the borrowed shape is a margin: a regular time where nothing has to be produced or proven. catching up is still making.

practice: Look at the coming week and find one day, or half a day if a whole one is impossible, that could be your margin. Ask three quiet questions: what small sign will mark its start, a phone put away, a lamp turned off?
Who else gets to rest because of it? And what one thing will you not do?

wordCard.voice: Secular sabbath. A weekly rest kept outside any religion, borrowing the shape of the Jewish sabbath: a regular time, a shared rest, a margin. Today's word.
